result.markdown: --- title: "Spherical Geometry in sf" format: clean-revealjs: css: misc/style-slides.css code-line-numbers: false footer: "[Home](../index.html)" include-in-header: misc/script.html title-slide-attributes: data-background-image: images/dflamini-crystal-ball-2090496_1280.png data-background-size: "contain" execute: echo: true warning: false message: false cache: true knitr: opts_chunk: tidy: false --- ::: {.cell} ::: ## Today 1. **S² and R²** — two models of space, one hidden default 2. **When flat breaks** — antimeridian rendering and predicate failures 3. **A polygon has two sides** — the core challenge of spherical geometry 4. **Semi-open boundaries** — why adjacent polygons share more than a border 5. **Discussion** — when does it matter in practice? # S² and R² {.subtitle} ## Two models of space :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **R² (flat)** - Points are (x, y) on an infinite plane - Used by GEOS — the geometry engine behind QGIS, PostGIS, sf historically - Assumes straight lines, Euclidean distances - Appropriate for **projected** CRS ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **S² (sphere)** - Points are (lon, lat) on a unit sphere - Used by **s2** — Google's C++ spherical geometry library, wrapped by the `s2` R package - Lines follow great circles; distances are geodesic - Appropriate for **geographic** CRS - Powers Google Maps, Earth Engine, and BigQuery GIS ::: :::: ## The switch - Since `sf` version 1.0 (2021), geographic coordinates automatically use s2 instead of GEOS. - Same function call; different geometry engine; potentially very different results - The switch affects: `st_area()`, `st_length()`, `st_distance()`, `st_buffer()`, all predicates ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sf_use_s2() # check current engine ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sf_use_s2(FALSE) # switch to GEOS (flat, R²) sf_use_s2(TRUE) # switch back to s2 (spherical, S²) ``` ::: :::{.notes} This is the key lever. When students see unexpected results with geographic data, checking `sf_use_s2()` is a good first step. Most of the time s2 gives the right answer; occasionally an operation isn't yet implemented and you need to fall back to GEOS. ::: ## When flat breaks: the antimeridian Same two endpoints — completely different rendering: ::: {.cell} ::: --- ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](spherical-geometry_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: :::{.notes} In R² the line is drawn as a straight horizontal segment from -170 to +170 going EAST across the globe — 340° of longitude on the flat map. In S², the same two points are connected by the short great-circle arc going WEST across the antimeridian — just 20°. Same two coordinates, completely different rendering. Note: st_length gives essentially the same result under both engines because GEOS also computes the minimum geodesic distance for a 2-point line; the difference shows up in how the geometry is drawn and in spatial operations on more complex shapes. ::: ## When flat breaks: predicates The same polygon, the same point — different answer: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sf_use_s2(FALSE) st_contains(pol, pole) # R²: pole is outside ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Sparse geometry binary predicate list of length 1, where the predicate was `contains' 1: (empty) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sf_use_s2(TRUE) st_contains(pol, pole) # S²: pole is inside ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Sparse geometry binary predicate list of length 1, where the predicate was `contains' 1: 1 ``` ::: ::: --- ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](spherical-geometry_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: :::{.notes} In R², the polygon edges are straight lines in equirectangular space. The three vertices form a small triangle that sits above the South Pole — the pole is clearly outside. In S², the edges follow great circles. Great-circle arcs between points in the southern hemisphere curve toward the pole, so the same three vertices enclose a much larger region that includes the South Pole. Same coordinates, opposite predicate result. Source: Pebesma & Dunnington (2020), "In r-spatial, the Earth is no longer flat". ::: # A polygon has two sides {.subtitle} ## Two regions from one ring In R²: a polygon ring encloses a **bounded** area. The outside extends to infinity — obviously "outside." In S²: a ring on a sphere divides it into **exactly two finite regions**. There is no infinity. Which side is "inside" depends entirely on **ring direction**. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Same 4 corners — different winding order sq_ccw <- st_sfc(st_polygon(list(matrix( # CCW → small region c(-10,-10, 10,-10, 10,10, -10,10, -10,-10), ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE))), crs = 4326) sq_cw <- st_sfc(st_polygon(list(matrix( # CW → large region c(-10,-10, -10,10, 10,10, 10,-10, -10,-10), ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE))), crs = 4326) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} units::set_units(st_area(sq_ccw), "km^2") # small square ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 4969697 [km^2] ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} units::set_units(st_area(sq_cw), "km^2") # rest of Earth ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 4969697 [km^2] ``` ::: ::: ## Ring direction - In S²: interior is the region **to the left** when walking the boundary - **CCW ring** (counter-clockwise) → interior is the small side — same as R² - **CW ring** (clockwise) → interior is the large side — the "rest of the globe" | Ring | R² behaviour | S² behaviour | |---|---|---| | CCW exterior | Standard polygon | Small-side interior | | CW exterior | Invalid / hole | Large-side interior | - `st_as_s2(x, oriented = FALSE)` auto-corrects ring direction, assuming the intended interior is **less than half the sphere** ## Stop and think You are building a global land cover database. One of the classes is **ocean**. > How would you represent the ocean as a geometry in a GIS? Discuss in pairs. Consider: - What are its boundaries? - Can you define it as a simple polygon in R²? - What about in S²? --- The ocean is the **complement** of all land polygons — it has no outer boundary, only inner ones. In R²: impossible to represent directly (unbounded exterior). In S²: the whole sphere **is** a valid polygon. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} land <- st_as_sf(s2_data_countries()) earth <- st_as_sfc("POLYGON FULL", crs = "EPSG:4326") ocean <- st_difference(earth, st_union(land)) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Fraction of Earth's surface covered by ocean as.numeric(st_area(ocean) / st_area(earth)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.288699 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](spherical-geometry_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: # Semi-open boundaries {.subtitle} ## The shared edge problem Adjacent polygons share an edge. Under S² (or GEOS with `model = "closed"`): - A point **on the shared edge** intersects **both** polygons - For spatial joins or point-in-polygon counts: double-counting ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Default: closed model — adjacent counties intersect each other st_intersects(nc[1:3, ], nc[1:3, ], sparse = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [1,] TRUE TRUE FALSE [2,] TRUE TRUE TRUE [3,] FALSE TRUE TRUE ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Semi-open: each county only intersects itself st_intersects(nc[1:3, ], nc[1:3, ], sparse = FALSE, model = "semi-open") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [1,] TRUE FALSE FALSE [2,] FALSE TRUE FALSE [3,] FALSE FALSE TRUE ``` ::: ::: --- The `model` parameter controls boundary inclusion: | Model | Boundary belongs to | Use when | |---|---|---| | `"closed"` (default) | Both polygons | Spatial filters, overlap detection | | `"open"` | Neither polygon | Points strictly inside only | | `"semi-open"` | Exactly one polygon | Coverage operations, point-in-polygon counts, raster analogy | The semi-open model mirrors how **raster grids** work: each cell owns its upper-left corner and upper/left edges — no gaps, no double-counting. # Practical consequences {.subtitle} ## How different are measurements? For typical geographic analyses: **negligible**. | Measure | Relative difference (s2 vs flat) | Absolute example | |---|---|---| | Area | ±0.007% | ~7 km² per 100 000 km² | | Length | ±0.013% | ~13 m per 100 km | | Distance | up to ~0.5% | ~1–2 km over 500 km | For continental or global scale: **not negligible**. The antimeridian is the clearest failure case. ## When to use each engine ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sf_use_s2(TRUE) # default — always correct for geographic CRS sf_use_s2(FALSE) # fall back to GEOS when: # • working with projected CRS (s2 adds no benefit) # • an operation is not yet in s2 (e.g. st_voronoi()) # • debugging: compare results between engines ``` ::: Rule of thumb: - **Geographic CRS (degrees)** → leave s2 on - **Projected CRS (metres)** → irrelevant which engine; GEOS is used anyway - **Operation fails or warns** → check if the operation is implemented in s2; fall back if needed # Discussion {.subtitle} ## Discussion challenge Your colleague downloads Swiss municipality boundaries in EPSG:4326 and runs: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} municipalities |> st_join(cantons, join = st_intersects) |> group_by(canton_id) |> summarise(total_pop = sum(pop)) ``` ::: Some municipalities on cantonal borders appear in **two** cantons and their population is counted twice. - What is causing this? - How do you fix it? - Are there cases where `model = "closed"` is actually the right choice? :::{.callout-important title="Discuss in groups"} No external sources — reason from what you know about s2 boundary models ::: ## References {#refs}

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
